samples.text:
The bar chart show how much electricity six countries produced from three renewable sources, which are hydro, wind and solar, in 2022.

Country A produced the most electricity. It generated 380 TWh from hydro, and this is much more than any other country. Its wind and solar was 70 and 40 TWh. Country E also used mainly hydro power with 140 TWh, but it had very little wind (15 TWh) and solar (5 TWh).

In Country B and Country D wind was the biggest source. Country B made 120 TWh of wind, 95 TWh of hydro and 60 TWh of solar. Country D produced 110 TWh from wind but only 20 TWh from hydro and 35 from solar.

Finally, solar was the most important in Country C and Country F. Country C had 90 TWh of solar, it is the highest solar figure, and Country F had 60 TWh. Country F produced only 8 TWh of hydro, which was the lowest in the chart.

Overall, hydro was the main source in Country A and E, but the other countries depend more on wind or solar power.
samples.why: Accurate figures for every country · overview present but brief and at the end · mechanical sequencing (Finally) · some awkward word choice · agreement, tense and punctuation errors that do not block meaning.

samples.text:
The chart compares the quantity of electricity that six countries generated from hydro, wind and solar power in 2022.

Overall, Country A generated far more renewable electricity than the other countries, mainly from hydro power. Each country tended to depend on one main source: hydro in Countries A and E, wind in B and D, and solar in C and F.

Country A's hydro output of 380 TWh was the highest figure on the chart and more than two and a half times that of Country E, the second-largest hydro producer at 140 TWh. Country A also generated 70 TWh from wind and 40 TWh from solar. In contrast, Country E produced very little from the other two sources, with only 15 TWh and 5 TWh respectively.

Wind was the leading source in Country B, at 120 TWh, and Country D, at 110 TWh, while hydro contributed 95 TWh and 20 TWh in these countries. As for solar, Country C generated the most, 90 TWh, which were considerably higher than its hydro (60 TWh) and wind (25 TWh) figures. Country F was the smallest producer overall, relying mostly on solar (60 TWh) and wind (45 TWh), with a hydro output of just 8 TWh.
samples.why: Clear overview grouping countries by main source · key features highlighted with accurate comparisons · logical progression and varied linking · good range of vocabulary · one minor agreement slip.

samples.text:
The bar chart provides a breakdown of renewable electricity generation in six countries in 2022, distinguishing between hydro, wind and solar power.

The most striking feature is the dominance of Country A, whose hydroelectric output alone exceeded the total renewable generation of any other country. Beyond this, the countries fall into three pairs according to their principal source: hydro in A and E, wind in B and D, and solar in C and F.

Country A generated 380 TWh from hydro, supplemented by a relatively modest 70 TWh from wind and 40 TWh from solar. Country E shared this reliance on hydro, producing 140 TWh, but its wind and solar output was minimal, at 15 TWh and a mere 5 TWh.

Wind was the leading source in Countries B and D, which generated 120 TWh and 110 TWh respectively. However, Country B had a far more balanced mix, with substantial hydro output (95 TWh), whereas Country D relied on hydro for only 20 TWh. Solar power, meanwhile, was most significant in Country C, reaching 90 TWh, the highest solar figure among the six countries, and in Country F, where it produced 60 TWh. Country F also recorded the lowest hydro figure overall, just 8 TWh.
samples.why: Skilful selection of key features, including a derived comparison · clear, well-placed overview · figures used precisely · cohesion managed well · wide, natural vocabulary · complex structures, error-free.
